The first customer after the funeral brought a coat with a missing button.

“Your mother always kept spares,” he said.

“I know.” He lowered his hand. “I’m sorry.”

She nearly gave the coat back. Instead, she looked beneath the counter, where the biscuit tins had always been.

The man waited while Mara searched.

“Did she charge you last time?” she asked.

“Sometimes she let me fix things instead. That shelf, for instance.”

Mara found four brown buttons wrapped in a scrap of lining. One matched.

She had not sewn anything in years. Her first attempt tangled; she cut it away. The man took a seat by the window without being asked.

On the second attempt, the needle passed cleanly through. She remembered her mother teaching her to leave a little room beneath a coat button, enough for the thick cloth to settle.

When she finished, the man put the coat on and fastened it.

“What do I owe you?”

Mara glanced at the shelf. It sagged at one end.

“Do you have time?” she asked.
